tasks_note: Fixed here rather than generated before each run: the groups are run on different days, and their figures only compare if every script is marked against the same question. It also keeps the writing_task tier out of the suite, whose calls are then the evaluator's alone.

cases.script:
In recent years the question of how museums should be funded has provoked considerable debate. Of the various considerations, I would argue that public access and long-term financial stability matter most.

Charging an entrance fee undoubtedly generates revenue, and it is tempting to assume that visitors who pay will value what they see more highly. However, the evidence points the other way. Where charges have been introduced, attendance among younger and less affluent visitors has fallen sharply, and once that habit of visiting is lost it proves remarkably difficult to recover. A charge also sends an implicit message about whom a museum is for, and that message is heard most clearly by precisely those it discourages. A museum that is financially secure but socially narrow has arguably failed in its purpose.

Corporate sponsorship, by contrast, offers a more promising route, provided it is properly regulated. Sponsors bring not only money but also expertise and publicity, and exhibitions that would otherwise never be mounted become possible. The obvious risk is that commercial interests begin to shape curatorial decisions, which is why transparent agreements setting out editorial independence are essential.

On balance, while sponsorship raises legitimate concerns, these can be managed through regulation, whereas the damage done by entrance charges to public access is far harder to undo. For that reason I believe funding models should prioritise free admission, supported where necessary by carefully governed private partnerships.
cases.stresses: perfect: a genuinely strong C1 answer, band 5 throughout
cases.source: reference marking run: 20/20, estimated scale 210, against a task on the same topic

cases.script:
Dear Director,

I am writing to complain about the evening course of Business English that I did in your school last month. I am very disappointed because the course was not like your website said.

In your website you promise that the groups have maximum eight students and that all the teachers are native speakers with a lot of experience. Also it says that every student receive a book and access to online exercises. Because of this I decided to pay 350 euros, which is a lot of money for me.

However, the reality was very different. In my group there was nineteen students, so it was impossible to speak in the class. The teacher changed three times in two weeks and the last one was a student of the university who didn't explain nothing, he only read from the book. Honestly, it was a disaster! Besides, I never received the book and the password for the exercises didn't work, although I sent two emails to the secretary.

For all these reasons, I would like that you give me back at least the half of the money. If it is not possible, I think the minimum is to let me do the next course for free, with a small group like you promise. I hope you will take my complaint serious, because I don't think other students deserve the same experience.

I look forward to hearing from you soon.

Yours faithfully,
Marta Ruiz

cases.script:
Proposal: How To Spend The Money

Intro
OK, so you asked us what to do with the cash, and honestly I've got loads of ideas! Here's the deal, boss.

What's missing right now
Let's be real: the common room is a total dump. The sofas are falling apart, there's nowhere to sit when it rains, and the so-called gym is basically one broken treadmill and a sad old bench. Students who don't play football have absolutely nothing to do at lunchtime, which is why half of them just hang around the car park staring at their phones.

Where the money should go
First, sort out the common room. Chuck out the old furniture, get some decent sofas and a couple of big tables where people can actually work together. Second, turn the empty storeroom next to the library into a proper fitness room with a few bikes, some weights and a mat area for yoga. It wouldn't cost a fortune, trust me. Finally, stick some covered benches in the courtyard, because getting soaked every lunchtime is no fun at all.

Why we'd all be better off
If you do this, people will actually want to hang around on campus. Students who aren't into team sports will finally get some exercise, and the ones who just want to chill or study together will have somewhere half-decent to do it. Happier students, better grades, everybody wins, right?

Anyway, that's my two cents. Hope you go for it - you won't regret it, I promise!
cases.stresses: communicative achievement: every point covered, headed sections and accurate, idiomatic English, but written to the principal like a message to a friend -- 'boss', 'total dump', 'my two cents'. Wrong register for a proposal to a decision-maker.

cases.script:
Report on the careers fair

Introduction
The purpose of this report is to describe the careers fair that took place in the sports hall on 12 March, and to suggest some improvements for next year.

The event
Around thirty organisations took part, including local companies, two universities and the army. Each one had a stand where students could ask questions and take leaflets. There were also four talks in the main hall, for example about how to write a CV and how to prepare a job interview. More than 400 students attended during the day.

Most useful parts
According to the students I spoke to, the most useful part were the talks, especially the one about CVs, because many of them had never wrote one before. Students also liked the possibility to speak directly with people who work in jobs they are interested in. However, some stands were quite boring, as the representatives just gave out leaflets and didn't really talk to anyone.

Suggestions for next year
Firstly, the fair should be longer, because the talks were at the same time and students had to choose between them. Secondly, it would be a good idea to invite more companies from areas like technology and design, which are very popular between students. Finally, the college could organise short practice interviews with real employers, which would be really cool.

Conclusion
To sum up, the fair was a great success and I think it should definitely be repeated next year with these changes.
cases.stresses: middle: a well-organised report that covers every point, with a few verb and preposition errors and some informal slips ('really cool') that weaken the impersonal register.

because the talks were at the same time

cases.script:
The Lighthouse Keepers: a mystery that rewards a second visit

Few series manage to be gripping the first time round and even better the second, but The Lighthouse Keepers pulls it off with apparent ease.

Set on a remote Scottish island, the six-part drama follows Isla, a young marine biologist who arrives to study seabirds and finds herself drawn into the disappearance of the island's last lighthouse keeper. What begins as a slow-burning puzzle gradually becomes a moving portrait of a tiny community bound together by secrets it would rather forget.

So why watch it twice? On a first viewing you are swept along by the plot, desperate to discover what happened on that stormy night in 1987. Only on a second viewing do you notice how carefully the writers have planted clues in plain sight: a half-finished letter on a kitchen table, a character who never quite answers a question. Scenes that seemed like quiet filler turn out to be crucial, and the final episode takes on an entirely new meaning.

The performances are superb throughout, and the windswept cinematography makes the island almost a character in its own right.

If you are looking for explosions and car chases, this is not the series for you. However, anyone who enjoys intelligent storytelling, atmospheric settings and endings that make you rethink everything you have seen should add it to their list without delay. Just make sure you have time to watch it all over again.
cases.stresses: high: an engaging review that describes, evaluates and recommends, with a wide range of structures (inversion, participle clauses) and no errors.

cases.script:
Museums are an important part of our culture, but they need a lot of money to work. There are different ways to get this money. In this essay I will talk about entrance charges and government funding.

On the one hand, many museums ask visitors to pay a ticket. This is a good way to get money because the people who visit the museum pay for it. Also, people sometimes value more the things that they pay for. However, tickets can be quite expensive, and some people, for example students or old people, cannot pay them. This is a problem because museums should be for everybody, not only for people with money.

On the other hand, the government can give money to museums. In this way the entrance can be free and more people can visit. I think this is very positive, especially for children, because they can learn a lot of things about history and art. The problem is that the government has to pay for many other things like hospitals and schools, so sometimes there is not enough money for museums.

In conclusion, I think that government funding is more important than entrance charges, because it helps more people to visit museums. But maybe museums can also ask for a small price for special exhibitions. In my opinion, it is important that everybody can enjoy museums and learn from them, and the government should help to make this possible.
cases.stresses: fair: answers the task fully -- two methods, and which matters more -- but with simple lexis, formulaic linkers and thin development. Calibrates the middle of the scale.

cases.script:
Hi Sam,

It was great to hear from you, and I'm thrilled you've finally decided to come over! A whole month here will do wonders for your Spanish, I promise.

First things first: accommodation. Rather than booking a hotel, I'd strongly recommend staying with a host family. My aunt's neighbours, the Morales, take in a student every summer, and they're the kind of people who'll drag you into every conversation whether you like it or not -- which is exactly what you need. If you'd prefer more independence, there are plenty of shared flats near the university that are surprisingly cheap in July.

As for meeting people, the best thing you could do is sign up for one of the language exchanges held in the cafés around the main square. They're relaxed, free and full of locals desperate to practise their English, so you'll end up swapping languages over coffee most evenings. I'd also suggest joining the hiking club; nobody can avoid chatting on a five-hour walk!

A couple of warnings, though. Don't underestimate the heat -- by mid-afternoon the streets are deserted, and you'll soon understand why everyone disappears for a siesta. And be prepared for people to talk at lightning speed. Don't be discouraged if you can't follow at first; by the second week it'll feel completely different.

Let me know your dates as soon as you've booked your flight, and I'll come and pick you up from the airport.

Can't wait to see you!

Lucía
cases.stresses: high: an informal email to a friend that covers all three points with precise, idiomatic language and a register exactly right for the reader. A marker that equates C1 with formality will under-mark it.

cases.script:
Proposal: a mentoring scheme for new students

Introduction
The purpose of this proposal is explain how a mentoring scheme can help to the new students of our college during their first months.

Problems of the new students
When I arrived to this college last year, I felt very lost. Many new students don't know where are the classrooms or how to use the online platform, and some of them are living far from their families for first time. Also, it is difficult to make friends, specially for the international students, because the groups are already formed.

How the scheme would work
My idea is that every new student have a mentor, who is a student of second or third year. The mentor would meet with him once a week during the first two months and would answer to his questions. They could also go together to the activities of the student association, so the new student knows more people. I think is better if the mentor studies the same subject, because he can give advices about the teachers and the exams.

What we need
To start the scheme, we need around thirty volunteers and a small room where the meetings can take place. Also, the college should give to the mentors a short training and maybe a certificate, so more students are interested to participate.

Recommendation
In my opinion, this scheme would be very useful and not very expensive. I recommend to start it in September, with the new course.

cases.script:
Report on the Language Exchange

Introduction
The exchange should be repeated. Twenty-four students took part. The partner school is in Lyon. Host families were found for all participants.

Activities
Most participants reported that their spoken French improved noticeably. Some found the host families' pace of speech difficult at first. A recommendation is that preparation sessions be held beforehand. Lessons took place every morning at the partner school. Visits were organised in the afternoons. The cost was considered reasonable by most families.

Usefulness
A trip to the Roman amphitheatre at Vienne was arranged. Several students would have preferred a longer stay. Students attended lessons in mathematics and history taught in French. Confidence in speaking was the area of greatest improvement. The weekends were spent with host families. A questionnaire was completed by all participants at the end of the fortnight.

Recommendations
Twelve students said it was the most valuable experience of their school career. Written skills improved less than oral skills. Lessons at the partner school were judged demanding but rewarding. The exchange lasted two weeks. Pairing students with similar interests would help. Two students experienced difficulties with their host families, which were resolved by the organising teacher. The partner school has expressed interest in a return visit next year. Funding for the coach journey was provided by the parents' association. It is suggested that the exchange be extended to three weeks.
cases.stresses: organisation: formal, impersonal and accurate, and every point is there, but the sentences are a list with no linking, and the findings sit under the wrong headings -- the recommendation opens the introduction, findings fill the recommendations section.
cases.source: written for this dataset; expected_bands are the author's target, not yet an examiner's marking

cases.script:
Wordly: learning Italian on the bus

Last year I decided to learn Italian before a trip to Rome, but I didn't have time for classes. A friend recommended me Wordly, an app that promises you can learn a language in only ten minutes a day, so I downloaded it and started immediately.

The app is very easy to use. Every day you do a short lesson with games, listening exercises and little tests. I used it mainly on the bus to work, and I must admit that it became a little addiction for me! The best thing is the voice recognition, which tells you if your pronunciation is correct. Thanks to this, when I arrived to Rome I could order food and ask directions without problems.

However, the app has also some weaknesses. The grammar explanations are very short, so sometimes I didn't understand why a sentence was wrong. Also, after a few months the exercises become a bit repetitive, and the conversations are not very realistic.

Is it worth to pay for the full version? The free version has adverts every few minutes, and the premium version costs eight euros per month. If you want to learn the basics for a holiday, the free version is enough. But if you are serious about learning, you should combine the app with a good grammar book.

All in all, Wordly is fun and practical, and I would recommend it to anyone who wants to start learning a language in their free time.
cases.stresses: middle: a lively review in the right register that answers every point, with a few verb-pattern and word-order errors, everyday lexis and simple linking.

expected_annotations.span: the app has also some weaknesses

cases.script:
Dear Ms Harper,

I am writing in connection with your recent announcement about the library on Station Road, a building which has played a central part in my life since I was a child.

I first walked through its doors at the age of six, holding my grandmother's hand, and I can still remember the smell of polished wood and the enormous windows that flood the reading room with light. The building itself, designed in 1904 by the architect Thomas Whitcombe, is one of the finest examples of Edwardian civic architecture in the region. Its carved stone entrance and the stained-glass panels above the main staircase deserve to be far better known than they are.

Over the years I have borrowed hundreds of books there, from adventure stories to the history texts that eventually led me to study archaeology. Several of the librarians have become friends, and I have attended many of the excellent evening talks organised by the local history society, which I would encourage anyone to join.

Naturally, I was disappointed to read about the reduced opening hours, as I sometimes visit in the evenings.

I would also like to take this opportunity to suggest that the library should publish a short illustrated guide to the building, so that visitors can appreciate its architectural heritage. Many residents walk past it every day without realising its significance.

Thank you for taking the time to read my letter. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Daniel Reyes
cases.stresses: content: a well-written, well-organised formal letter that spends itself on the library's architecture and the writer's memories. It mentions the effect on the writer in one sentence, suggests no saving, and its only request is irrelevant. The reader is minimally informed.

Proposal for the redevelopment of Victoria Gardens

Introduction
The aim of this proposal is to outline how Victoria Gardens, currently one of the most neglected spaces in the town centre, could be transformed into a park that residents genuinely want to use.

Current situation
At present, the gardens are rarely visited except as a shortcut to the station. The flowerbeds have been left to grow wild, several benches are broken, and the poor lighting means that many people, particularly older residents, avoid the area after dark. The children's play area was closed two years ago and has never been replaced.

Suggested improvements
Firstly, the lighting along the main paths should be upgraded, which would make the park feel considerably safer in the evenings. Secondly, I would recommend replacing the old play area with a modern one designed for a wider age range. Finally, part of the lawn could be set aside for a community garden, where local volunteers and schools could grow vegetables and flowers.

Benefits
These changes would bring the park back into everyday use. Families would have somewhere safe for children to play within walking distance of their homes, while the community garden would give people of different generations a reason to meet. In addition, a well-maintained park would make the surrounding shops and cafés more attractive to visitors.

Recommendation
I strongly recommend that the council prioritise the lighting and the play area, as these would have the most immediate impact, and consult residents before finalising the design of the garden.
cases.stresses: high: a proposal with headings, a formal persuasive register and a closing recommendation, covering the three points with precise, accurate language.

Report on the members' survey

Introduction
This report summarises the responses to last month's survey, which was completed by 142 members, and makes recommendations for attracting new users to the centre.

Strengths
Members were overwhelmingly positive about the staff, with almost nine in ten describing instructors as knowledgeable and approachable. The swimming pool was also singled out for praise, particularly since the changing rooms were refurbished last spring. A number of respondents mentioned that the centre's membership fees compare favourably with those of private gyms in the area.

Main complaints
By far the most common complaint concerned overcrowding in the gym between six and eight in the evening, when several machines are often out of order. Many members also expressed frustration at the online booking system, which frequently crashes and does not allow classes to be cancelled. Finally, parents noted that there are very few activities for teenagers, who tend to drift away from sport at that age.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, it is recommended that the centre:
- introduce off-peak discounts to spread demand more evenly across the day;
- replace or repair faulty equipment as a matter of priority;
- upgrade the booking system so that members can manage their own bookings;
- launch a programme of activities aimed specifically at teenagers, such as climbing and dance.

Conclusion
Overall, members value the centre highly. If the issues above are addressed, it should be well placed to retain its current members and attract new ones.
cases.stresses: high: an impersonal report with headings, findings drawn from the survey and recommendations that follow from them, in accurate, varied language.

La Terraza: a perfect place for celebrate

Last month my parents was celebrating their twenty-five years of marriage, so all the family we went to La Terraza, a small restaurant near of the old harbour. I had read many good comments in internet and I wanted that the night was special for them.

The restaurant is not very big but it is very nice. It have a terrace with views to the sea and in the inside there are old photos of fishermans in the walls. When we arrived, the waiter explained us the menu with a lot of patience, and even my grandmother, who don't speak English, could to understand everything.

About the food, I must to say it was the better fish I have ever eaten. We ordered a grilled sea bass for share and some vegetables, and every plates were delicious. The only problem was the dessert, it was too much sweet for my taste and very little. Also the prices is a bit high, but I think it worth it for a special occasion.

The service was the best part of the night. The staff were very kind with us and when they knew that it was my parents anniversary, they bringed a small cake with candles without we asked. My mother was crying of happiness!

In conclusion, I recommend La Terraza for everyone who want to celebrate something important. It is not cheap, but the food and the atmosphere makes you feel like at home. Sure we will come back.

annotations: expected_annotations are the errors the annotate node must find: a span of the script, its category, and 'also' for the other categories a defensible reading allows. At most eight per script, the clearest and most costly: the node reports at most twelve and chooses which, so a script with more real errors leaves it room to pick others without losing recall. tolerated_annotations are spans it may annotate or not, which count neither way: the remaining real slips, and debatable ones. Every real error must be in one list or the other, or annotating it would count as a false positive. A script with no expected error is clean for the annotator, whatever its bands. Organisation and content problems are not located errors, so the report and the letter have none.
